content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a document in 2019 on infection prevention and control, which is accessible online. This document provides comprehensive guidance on strategies to prevent infections in healthcare settings. 2. In 2006, WHO released a framework for making strategic choices in health systems to improve the quality of care. This document outlines processes for enhancing healthcare delivery and is available in PDF format. 3. WHO's 2018 vision for primary healthcare in the 21st century emphasizes achieving universal health coverage and aligning with sustainable development goals. This vision document is available online in PDF format. 4. The WHO Regional Office for Europe issued a declaration in 2017 during the Sixth Ministerial Conference on Environment and Health, focusing on improving environmental health standards, including water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities. 5. The UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water (GLAAS) 2018/2019 country survey document, published by WHO, provides insights into global WASH conditions and is available online. 6. WHO's fourth edition of the Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, published in 2011, offers detailed recommendations for ensuring safe drinking water. This document is accessible online. 7. WHO's 2018 Guidelines on Sanitation and Health provide evidence-based recommendations for improving sanitation in healthcare and other institutional settings. This document is available online. 8. A 2018 study by Weber et al. evaluated the implementation of the WASH FIT tool in Togo, demonstrating its effectiveness in strengthening healthcare facilities through WASH improvements. The findings were published in the journal Health Security. 9. WHO has established global minimum standards for environmental health in healthcare facilities, defining a basic level of service that includes key conditions in water, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, and environmental cleaning. 10. WHO and UNICEF have developed a set of questions to classify healthcare facilities based on service ladders for WASH, enabling global monitoring and inter-country comparability. 11. Countries are encouraged to define higher levels of WASH services and monitor corresponding indicators, such as the availability of cleaning protocols and staff training in cleaning practices. 12. Improved water sources, such as piped water, boreholes, protected wells, and rainwater, are designed to deliver safe water. Similarly, improved sanitation facilities, such as flush toilets connected to septic systems or dry pit latrines, are designed to hygienically separate human excreta from contact. 13. Healthcare facilities, whether in urban or rural areas, range from basic health posts to comprehensive primary care centers. Secondary and tertiary facilities provide more specialized care and should prioritize WASH investments, especially in facilities where births occur. 14. WASH practices include regular handwashing by healthcare providers, patients, and families, as well as routine cleaning of surfaces, floors, walls, toilets, and other areas in healthcare settings. 15. Infection prevention and control (IPC) is a scientific and practical approach to preventing harm caused by infections in healthcare settings. Effective IPC programs must be integrated with functional WASH services to reduce infections and combat antimicrobial resistance (AMR). 16. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when microorganisms develop the ability to resist the effects of antimicrobials, rendering standard treatments ineffective. Poor infection control and inadequate sanitation contribute to the spread of AMR. 17. Universal health coverage (UHC) ensures that all individuals and communities receive the health services they need without financial hardship. Achieving UHC is impossible without adequate WASH services. 18. Quality of care refers to the extent to which healthcare services improve desired health outcomes. WHO has developed standards and guidelines to enhance the quality of care, including maternal and newborn care, surgical site infection prevention, and IPC programs. 19. WHO's WASH FIT tool and other resources, such as the IPC assessment framework (IPCAF) and the global action plan on AMR, provide practical steps for improving WASH and IPC in healthcare facilities. 20. The Protocol on Water and Health is an international agreement aimed at protecting human health through better water management. It promotes universal access to safe drinking water and sanitation, with a focus on institutional settings like schools and healthcare facilities. 21. Serbia has integrated WASH indicators into its national monitoring program for communicable disease prevention, improving sanitary and hygienic conditions in healthcare facilities. This initiative aligns with global commitments under the Protocol on Water and Health. 22. WHO Regional Offices have embedded WASH standards into broader strategies for achieving UHC, managing emergencies, and addressing climate resilience. These efforts include national surveys, training programs, and policy integration. 23. The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) developed global indicators for WASH in healthcare facilities in 2018, which are used to track progress on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and inform national health monitoring systems. 24. The UN-Water GLAAS survey tracks policy implementation on WASH in healthcare facilities, holding countries accountable for collecting accurate data and taking action. The 2018–2019 cycle included questions on policies, budgets, and measures to address AMR and quality of care. 25. Serbia's participation in the GLAAS survey revealed data gaps and the need for improved WASH monitoring at national and local levels. This led to the inclusion of advanced service level indicators and immediate improvement measures in healthcare facilities.
